prompt: A six-person operations team is renamed Site Reliability Engineering. It still receives unbounded tickets, performs manual worker restarts, owns every deployment, and is blamed for every outage. It spends 78 percent of available time on reactive work, receives sixty mostly unactionable pages each week, has no user-journey SLO, and cannot require developers to fix production defects. Explain why the rename is not an SRE transformation. Separate operations, toil, engineering, and overhead; identify the first operating-model failures; propose a safe ninety-day recovery sequence; name measurements, owners, stop conditions, and proof limits; and explain what should not be automated first.
directAnswer: The team has an SRE title but not an SRE operating model. SRE is not defined by owning every operational task; it applies software engineering, explicit user reliability objectives, shared incentives, measured risk, sustainable response, and recurring-work reduction across the service lifecycle. Seventy-eight percent reactive work means the system has left too little protected engineering capacity to remove its sources of load. Some reactive work may be necessary non-toil operations, but manual repetitive automatable restarts and copied tickets that grow with demand are strong toil candidates. Sixty pages are delivery volume, not sixty incidents; without actionability, unique-event, acknowledgement, and missed-event data, page quality is unknown. Start by protecting users and responders: establish an escalation path and minimum coverage, inventory work and pages without blaming individuals, define one critical user journey and provisional SLI/SLO with product and development owners, assign code/change/capacity/security/on-call decisions, and stop accepting unowned work. Rank recurring sources by user risk, frequency, duration, growth, and safe removability. Remove the highest-risk source at its cause, beginning with tested worker self-recovery only after defining failure detection, bounded retries, idempotency, abort, manual override, telemetry, and rollback. Do not automate an ambiguous access ticket or blind restart first; that scales bad policy and can create security or retry harm. Review weekly: user SLI, page actionability, time to acknowledge/action, toil hours by source, engineering fraction, change failures, ownership gaps, and automation outcomes. Ninety days can establish a controlled recovery trajectory, but it cannot prove a mature SRE culture, durable skill, complete incident coverage, or production readiness without longer evidence and independent review.
foundation: Operations is work required to keep a service functioning, including legitimate judgement-heavy response. Toil is not simply boring work: it commonly has several properties such as manual execution, repetition, predictability, tactical response, automation potential, little enduring value, and growth with service demand. Engineering changes the system or operating mechanism so future work, risk, capacity, or capability improves. Overhead includes planning, meetings, training, and administration; it can be valuable and should not be hidden inside toil. SRE combines user-relevant reliability contracts, software engineering, production responsibility, shared ownership, risk decisions, observability, sustainable on-call, and learning loops. Renaming a team changes none of those mechanisms.
reasoningSteps: Begin with the user and responder symptoms rather than the team label: unknown customer reliability, sixty low-actionability pages, and 78 percent reactive load.
Define the work categories before calculating them so disliked engineering, necessary incidents, and administrative overhead are not all mislabeled toil.
Identify manual restarts and copied tickets as toil candidates because they are repetitive, tactical, automatable, low-enduring-value, and demand-scaled; confirm with measured occurrences and time.
Treat the missing user SLO as an incentive and decision gap: nobody can say how much reliability is enough, whether change risk is acceptable, or which work protects users most.
Treat absent developer responsibility and universal SRE ownership as a feedback-loop failure: the people able to change code are insulated from production consequences.
Stabilize human safety and service coverage before reducing pages or rejecting work; retain escalation and critical user-symptom detection.
Create a work and alert inventory with population, duration, owner, trigger, user impact, risk, recurrence, growth, action, and outcome rather than ranking only by annoyance.
Agree one user journey, provisional SLI/SLO, and explicit product, development, SRE, security, capacity, change, and incident responsibilities.
Select source removal using risk-adjusted return: recurring hours and reduced incident risk minus build, maintenance, adoption, failure, security, and opportunity costs.
Canary the chosen control with bounded authority, idempotency, observability, abort, rollback, and a retained manual path; verify user and operator outcomes independently.
Review weekly and adjust intake, staffing, on-call, engineering allocation, objectives, and ownership based on evidence rather than an arbitrary automation count.
State that ninety-day improvement and fixture arithmetic do not establish organizational transformation, individual performance, or mastery.
seniorAnswer: I would declare two coupled reliability risks: the customer service lacks a decision contract, and the team operating it has an unsustainable control loop. A title change cannot substitute for SLOs with consequences, software engineering capacity, shared production ownership, or workload regulation. My first week would preserve critical response coverage, provide a clear escalation path, and freeze only new unowned intake—not abandon existing incidents. I would sample and classify four weeks of tickets, pages, deployments, incidents, interrupts, overhead, and engineering work with team review. Manual restarts and copied access work are probable toil, but classification requires context and risk. In parallel, product, development, and SRE would define the highest-value user journey, good/total population, provisional objective, error-budget response, and a decision map for code, change, capacity, security, incident command, and on-call. During weeks two through six, we would remove the highest-risk recurring source, likely worker recovery, using a tested state machine with idempotency, retry bounds, rate limits, audit, manual override, canary, abort, and rollback—not a cron job that hides failures. Developers would share on-call or an equivalent production feedback obligation and own code defects. During weeks seven through twelve, we would measure user SLI, significant-event coverage, page precision/recall where ground truth exists, pages per incident, acknowledge/action time, toil hours, engineering fraction, automation failure, and responder health. We would reject a target that merely makes a dashboard green and would renegotiate workload or service support if protected engineering time cannot recover. Success is a measured, owned improvement trajectory with safer users and humans; it is not a new team name or a one-quarter maturity claim.
weakAnswer: Automate all tickets, silence noisy alerts, and tell the new SRE team to spend half its time coding.
whyWeak: It automates unknown policy and potentially privileged mistakes, destroys symptom coverage without measuring missed incidents, treats a time allocation as a command rather than an operating constraint, ignores user objectives and developer ownership, provides no safe rollout or rollback, and blames the team for a system of incentives it does not control.

evidence.signal: The team spends 78 percent of available time on reactive work.
evidence.proves: Under the stated classification and window, only 22 percent remains for all other work.
evidence.doesNotProve: That every reactive hour is toil, who caused the load, individual productivity, or the correct universal engineering fraction.

evidence.signal: Manual worker restarts and copied tickets recur and grow with demand.
evidence.proves: The tasks exhibit several classic toil properties and merit measured source-removal review.
evidence.doesNotProve: That immediate automation is safe, cheaper, authorized, or better than eliminating the triggering defect or policy.

evidence.signal: Sixty mostly unactionable pages arrive weekly.
evidence.proves: The declared notification and human-interruption load is high.
evidence.doesNotProve: Sixty unique incidents, false-positive count, recall, missed significant events, or the safe set of rules to remove.

evidence.signal: No user-journey SLO or error-budget policy exists.
evidence.proves: The scenario lacks an explicit shared reliability decision contract.
evidence.doesNotProve: That users are currently harmed, what target they need, or that an SLO alone changes incentives.

evidence.signal: Developers neither share production response nor own code defects.
evidence.proves: The stated ownership model separates change authority from important operational feedback.
evidence.doesNotProve: Developer intent, capability, or that one prescribed on-call structure fits the organization.

followUps.answer: No. Novel diagnosis, a rare high-judgement migration, training, design review, and an incident command action can be manual yet provide enduring value or resist safe automation. Classify using multiple properties and context.

followUps.prompt: Why not enforce exactly 50 percent engineering time tomorrow?
followUps.answer: A target can expose an unhealthy system, but abrupt enforcement can drop response coverage. Stabilize risk, measure categories, remove or renegotiate sources, adjust staffing and scope, and protect engineering capacity through an agreed operating policy.

followUps.prompt: Should developers always carry the pager?
followUps.answer: They need meaningful production feedback and responsibility, but the exact rotation depends on service criticality, staffing, competence, hours, legal context, and escalation design. Shared ownership is the invariant; one universal roster is not.

rubric.observableEvidence: Explains why title, tooling, and universal operational ownership do not constitute SRE.
Separates operations, toil, engineering, and overhead using multiple toil properties.
Establishes a user journey, provisional SLI/SLO, consequence policy, and business owner.
Reconnects code/change authority, production feedback, escalation, and shared decisions.
Protects service and human coverage before intake, alert, or automation changes.
Ranks source removal by risk-adjusted benefit and includes canary, abort, rollback, and control limits.
Names matched user, work, alert, change, ownership, and human sustainability measures.
Rejects blame, unsupported causality, universal prescriptions, and maturity inflation.
